disease_info: Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type) is characterized by a combination of mood episodes meeting criteria for mania (and often depression) together with psychotic symptoms such as delusions or hallucinations, where psychotic features also occur for a substantial period independent of mood episodes. The bipolar type specifically involves at least one manic episode, and the course is often chronic or recurrent, with fluctuating mood and psychosis leading to functional impairment in work, relationships, and self‑care. It is distinguished from Bipolar I Disorder with psychotic features by the persistence of psychotic symptoms outside of mood episodes, and from Schizophrenia by the presence of prominent mood episodes for a significant portion of the illness. Onset commonly occurs in late adolescence or early adulthood but can emerge or become clinically evident later in life under accumulating stressors, medical changes, or role transitions.

narrative.stressor: About a year and a half ago, Gloria’s carefully ordered life was disrupted when her husband developed complications from long‑standing diabetes and needed multiple hospitalizations, leaving her as his primary caregiver while still working full‑time supervising housekeeping teams. The added responsibilities eroded her usual routines—early morning hikes, church groups, and meticulous checklists at work—and she began staying up late monitoring his blood sugars and medications, gradually becoming more keyed up and overextended. Over the next year and two months, coworkers and her supervisor noticed that her previously reliable judgment and calm demeanor gave way to increasingly erratic decisions about supplies and schedules, leading to conflicts on the job and concern from her church friends, who saw her withdraw from social activities. She finally came to psychiatric attention after an incident where she became so preoccupied and disorganized at work that she left several client homes half‑finished and got lost driving a familiar route, prompting her employer and pastor to urge her and her husband to seek professional evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My thoughts feel all jumbled and I can’t keep my words or plans straight anymore, even for simple tasks I’ve done for years.”

narrative.stressor: Eric had been gradually scaling up an ambitious regenerative agriculture project, taking on new debt to integrate AI‑driven systems and drones into the family farm just as commodity prices became volatile and weather patterns unpredictable. Around this time, about 14 months before presentation, he threw himself into nonstop planning and public outreach—late‑night coffee, expanded workshops, and aggressive expansion plans—until his wife and adult children noticed his workdays stretching into the early morning and his business decisions becoming increasingly risky and out of step with their financial reality. Over the following year, his behavior at community meetings and on the farm grew more erratic; he clashed with long‑time collaborators, made abrupt changes to planting schedules, and seemed unable to back down from ideas that others found unrealistic, leading to mounting financial strain and tension within the family partnership. The tipping point came when he insisted on pursuing a major equipment purchase despite clear budget constraints and refused to revise his plans, prompting his family and the farm’s accountant to insist on a medical evaluation, which led to psychiatric referral.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m absolutely certain I’m seeing things more clearly than everyone else and that my ideas can’t be wrong, even when my family says they make no sense.”

narrative.stressor: Dawn’s difficulties began to surface after she moved from a stable gallery position into full‑time freelance work and curating her own shows in Las Vegas, a transition she had long planned but that left her income unpredictable and her schedule unstructured. Initially energized by the creative freedom, she started taking on too many projects at once, staying up most nights working on intricate mixed‑media pieces and planning an immersive exhibition that blended her art with elaborate sound and light elements. Over roughly the next year, friends and collaborators noticed her becoming increasingly intense and hard to reach between bursts of productivity, missing meetings or appearing preoccupied and guarded during studio visits, which led to frayed professional relationships and a stalled major exhibit. When she began canceling hikes and yoga classes she once relied on for balance and confided to a close friend that her mind felt like it was “running too fast to keep up with,” the friend helped her arrange an appointment with a community mental health clinic attached to an arts nonprofit.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My thoughts won’t slow down—they’re racing all the time and I can’t turn them off long enough to focus or rest.”
